title: Rehat and humility
hookLine: keeping the code does not make one better than others

lines: A GLANCE AT THE ONES ASLEEP.
KEEPING A RULE, OR KEEPING SCORE?
cards: Any rule kept well comes with a small, quiet danger. Someone starts running at dawn and, a month later, catches themselves glancing at the people still asleep.
Someone gives up sugar and starts noticing everyone else's dessert. Keeping a discipline can turn, without anyone meaning it to, into keeping score.
A code as full as the Rehat Maryada could make that danger bigger: a Sikh who keeps every line might be tempted to look sideways at a cousin who doesn't. The hymns speak to that danger.

teach.b: Early on this path you met sweetness and humility side by side. Here's how deep it goes.
Guru Arjan, in the Sukhmani Sahib on Ang 266, says, in paraphrase: the one who knows themselves to be lowly is counted the highest of all.
The ladder is turned upside down; climbing it by your own effort, and announcing it, sends you down. Then Kabir, whose verses sit in the Guru Granth Sahib beside the Gurus' own.

teach.h: ANG 1364: KABIR, THE WORST OF ALL.
teach.b: On Ang 1364, in paraphrase, Kabir says: I am the worst of all; everyone else is good. Whoever understands this, he adds, is a friend of mine. A saint whose words are sung in gurdwaras calls himself the worst.
Then a story Sikh tradition tells about the founding of the Khalsa.

teach.h: THE GURU KNEELS TO THE FIVE.
teach.b: Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh gave amrit to the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones, then knelt before those same five and asked them to give amrit to him.
A line traditionally sung about that day calls him the Guru and the disciple at once. So the founder of the Khalsa put himself under its vow, and under the very people he'd just initiated.
Read beside these three, the code looks like a way to shape a life toward God, not a ranking of who's closer.
A Sikh can keep every line and still sit in the langar in the same row as everyone else, eating the same food from the same hands.

teach.h: THE RULE SHAPES ME, NOT MY VIEW OF YOU.
teach.b: The rule shapes the one who keeps it. It doesn't make them a judge of anyone who doesn't.

how: Sikh teaching sets humility (nimrata) beside the rehat; in the langar, amritdhari and non-amritdhari Sikhs and visitors sit in the same rows and eat the same food.

o: keeping the code without ranking yourself higher
giving away your things so you stay humble
bowing low to elders as a rule of the code

games.q: inside rehat and humility: tap the pairs.
p: Kabir: I am the worst of all
gave amrit to the Guru, in the story
the same row, the same food

s: keeping the whole code makes a Sikh higher than others
the Sukhmani turns that around: the one who knows themselves lowly is counted the highest.
Kabir's verse calling himself the worst is in the Guru Granth Sahib
on Ang 1364: I am the worst of all; everyone else is good.
in the story, the Guru gave amrit but never received it
tradition says he knelt before the five and received amrit from them.

games.q: you're Guru Gobind Singh. you've just given amrit to five Sikhs and founded the Khalsa. what do you do next?
o: stand above them as the one who initiated them.
kneel and ask the five to give amrit to you.
send them out and keep the vow for them alone.
games.why: tradition says the Guru knelt before the five and received amrit from them, Guru and disciple at once.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you do well and keep up, a habit, a skill, a prayer, and let yourself be glad about it for a moment.
Then bring to mind someone who doesn't do that thing, and notice, without scolding, whether a little score-keeping shows up. Hold that person with the same warmth you just gave your own practice.

wordCard.voice: Rehat and humility. Keeping the Sikh code doesn't make anyone better than others. The Sukhmani calls the lowly the highest, Kabir calls himself the worst, and tradition says the Guru knelt to his own five. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: humility. Sikh teaching sets it beside every discipline.

carryVoice: Your line: no better than others. The Guru knelt to his own five. Rest well.
